meaning: To notice or become aware of something or some fact. It can also mean to come to, or to snap back to reality.
connection: Noun / 〜こと・〜の + に気がつく (also 「に気づく」)

senses.label: Notice something
senses.meaning: You notice a person or thing in front of you: "notice, spot". Usually it happens by chance, not because you were looking for it.
senses.connection: Noun + に気がつく／に気がついた／に気がつかない
examples: I noticed my friend at the station and called out to them.
I realized my wallet was gone.
He didn't seem to notice me.

senses.label: Realize a fact
senses.meaning: You become aware of a fact or truth: "realize, become aware". 「〜ことに」 or 「〜のに」 turns a whole clause into the object.
senses.connection: Plain-form clause + こと／の + に気がつく (often 「に気づく」)
examples: Only later did I realize I had taken the wrong road.
I realized my own mistake.

senses.label: Come to / snap out of it
senses.meaning: Without 「に」, 「気がつく」 can mean regaining consciousness, or snapping back to reality. 「気がつくと」 / 「気がついたら」 means "before I knew it, (it was already...)".
senses.connection: 気がつくと／気がついたら + unexpected result
examples: Before I knew it, it was already morning.
When I came to, I was in a hospital bed.

notes: The thing you notice takes 「に」, not 「を」: ✕「ミスを気がついた」→ ○「ミスに気がついた」. 「気づく」 also takes 「に」.
Don't confuse it with 「気をつける」 (be careful, watch out); the meaning is completely different. To say "watch out for cars": ✕「車に気がついてください」→ ○「車に気をつけてください」.
Saying 「〜に気がつきませんでしたか」 to a boss or client sounds like you're blaming them for being careless, which is rude. The honorific form is 「お気づきになる」; to point out a problem, you can say 「〜の点、ご確認いただけますか」.
When Japanese people fail to notice someone's needs, they often apologize with 「気がつかなくて、すみません」. 「気がつく人」 is praise meaning "a thoughtful, attentive person", not "a person who noticed something".

daily.title: Forgot something after leaving home
daily.description: You realize halfway there that you forgot something.
daily.example: After leaving home, I realized I had forgotten my umbrella.

daily.title: Running into someone on the street
daily.description: Telling your family you saw your teacher on the street.
daily.example: I noticed my teacher on the street and said hello.

daily.title: Lost track of time watching a drama
daily.description: Absorbed in something, you look up and time has flown.
daily.example: I was watching a drama, and before I knew it, it was 2 a.m.

work.title: Spotting an error in a document
work.description: Reporting to your boss a problem you found.
work.example: I noticed that the figures in the document are wrong.

work.title: Thanking a colleague
work.description: A colleague pointed out something you missed.
work.example: I hadn't noticed that point either. Thank you.

etymology: 「気」 means mind or attention, and 「つく」 means "to attach, to arise". Literally "your mind attaches to something", hence "to notice". 「気づく」 is a compound verb formed by dropping 「が」 from 「気が付く」.

similar.title: 〜ような気がする
similar.explanation: Same root: both are built on 「気」 (mind, feeling). 「〜ような気がする」 means "I have a feeling that...", and the content isn't necessarily certain; 「〜に気がつく」 means actually noticing a fact. 「間違えたような気がする」 (I feel like I made a mistake) ↔「間違えたことに気がついた」 (I realized I had made a mistake).

similar.title: 〜がわかる・〜ができる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「わかる」 means figuring out the content or understanding the reason; 「気がつく」 only means something you hadn't noticed has entered your awareness, without necessarily understanding it. 「間違いがわかった」 leans toward "I figured out what was wrong"; 「間違いに気がついた」 leans toward "I noticed there was a mistake".

similar.title: 〜が見える・〜が聞こえる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both describe perception that happens without effort. 「〜が見える／聞こえる」 is simply your eyes or ears picking something up; 「〜に気がつく」 is noticing at the level of awareness. You can see something and still not notice it: 「見えていたのに気がつかなかった」.

formation: It is made of 「に」 + 「気」 + 「が」 + 「つく」. 「気」 is your mind or attention, and 「つく」 means "to attach, to arise". Together they mean "your mind attaches itself to something": something that wasn't in your awareness enters it, hence "to notice, to become aware". The subject of the phrase is 「気」, so it's your mind attaching on its own; that's why it describes noticing naturally or by chance, not actively searching. 「に」 marks where your attention arrives, so the object can only take 「に」, never 「を」. With no object, 「気がつく」 means "your awareness comes back to you", which extends to "come to, snap out of it". 「気づく」 is the single verb formed by dropping 「が」.

meaning: Deliberately not doing something so things stay as they are, or holding off on doing it for now.
connection: Verb nai-form + でおく (written: 〜ずにおく; casual: 〜ないどく)

senses.label: Deliberately not do
senses.meaning: After thinking it over, you choose not to do something and leave things as they are: "purposely not ~, leave ~ undone". There's often a purpose behind it.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + でおく／でおいた／でおこう
examples: I won't tell Mom about this.
Please leave the window open.
I let the sleeping child sleep.

senses.label: Hold off for now
senses.meaning: Considering what comes later, you don't do it for now: "not ~ for the time being". Often used with 「今日は」「今は」「まだ」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + でおきます／ずにおく
examples: I won't buy it today. I'll come back another time.
Let's not draw a conclusion yet.

notes: Don't mix it up with 「〜ておく」; the meaning is the exact opposite: 「母には言っておこう」 is "I'll tell Mom in advance", while 「母には言わないでおこう」 is "I won't tell Mom for now".
The connection is nai-form + 「でおく」; you can't use 「なくて」: ✕「言わなくておく」→ ○「言わないでおく」.

「〜ないでおく」 carries a deliberate intention, with the future in mind. When something simply hasn't been done, use 「〜ないでいる」: 「ずっと連絡しないでいる」 (I still haven't contacted them) describes an ongoing situation, not a deliberate choice.

The casual contraction 「〜ないどく」 is only for family and friends; to a boss or client it sounds too casual. To ask someone to keep from doing something, 「〜ないでおいていただけますか」 is more polite than 「〜ないでおいてください」.

daily.title: Keeping a friend's secret
daily.description: A friend asks you not to tell anyone, and you agree.
daily.example: Got it, I won't tell anyone.

daily.title: Hesitating while shopping
daily.description: A clerk recommends something; the customer decides not to buy for now.
daily.example: I'm just looking today, so I'll hold off on buying.

daily.title: Leaving the room as it is
daily.description: A family member asks you not to touch things before going out.
daily.example: Leave the papers on the desk as they are, OK?

work.title: Not going public yet
work.description: A meeting decides not to explain to the client yet.
work.example: Let's not tell the client about this yet.

work.title: Leaving settings unchanged
work.description: During a handover, a colleague explains a setting was left as is on purpose.
work.example: I deliberately left the settings unchanged.

etymology: Made of the negative 「〜ない」 + 「で」 (linking a state) + 「おく」. 「おく」 originally means "to put, to place" and expresses keeping a state going, so 「ないでおく」 is "keeping the state of not doing".

similar.title: 〜ておく
similar.explanation: Same root: both are built on 「おく」 (put down, handle something for later), and both carry the intention of thinking ahead. The difference is doing vs. not doing: 「〜ておく」 means doing something in advance (「ビールを冷やしておく」), while 「〜ないでおく」 means deliberately not doing it for now (「ビールを開けないでおく」).

similar.title: 〜ないで (without doing)
similar.explanation: Same root: both contain 「〜ないで」. 「〜ないで」 simply means "do something else without doing ..." (「朝ご飯を食べないで出かける」), with no sense of deliberately keeping things that way for later; 「〜ないでおく」 isn't followed by another action, and its focus is on deliberately not doing something.

similar.title: 〜まま
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both can express leaving things as they are. 「〜ままにしておく」 focuses on the state not changing (「窓を開けたままにしておく」); 「〜ないでおく」 focuses on not performing an action (「窓を閉めないでおく」).

formation: It is made of a verb nai-form + 「で」 + 「おく」. 「〜ないで」 means "in a state of not doing ...", and 「おく」 originally means "to put, to place"; in 「〜ておく」 it extends to "take care of something and leave it for later". Together they mean "leave the state of not doing as it is", so it expresses deliberately not doing something and keeping things the way they are. Since 「おく」 itself carries the intention "for later", the meaning "not doing it for the time being" follows naturally. The written 「〜ずにおく」 simply replaces 「ないで」 with the literary 「ずに」; the structure and meaning are the same.

meaning: A sentence-initial conjunction that adds another item or reason of the same kind: "besides, on top of that, what's more".

senses.label: Adding a similar point
senses.meaning: Adds another piece of information in the same direction: "also, what's more". Both parts are usually both positive or both negative.
examples: This place is cheap. And the food is good, too.
It's cold today, and on top of that it's windy.
He's kind. And he's very hardworking, too.

senses.label: Adding a reason
senses.meaning: When giving reasons, adds one more: "besides, anyway". Sentences often end in 「〜し」 or 「〜から」.
senses.connection: Reason A。それに、reason B + し／から
examples: I'm not going today. Besides, it's raining.
It's late, let's go home. Besides, we have to get up early tomorrow, too.

notes: Both sentences must point in the same direction (both pluses or both minuses); it can't express contrast: ✕「この店は安い。それに、まずい。」→ ○「この店は安い。でも、まずい。」
It doesn't express time order: ✕「ご飯を食べた。それに、歯を磨いた。」→ ○「ご飯を食べた。それから、歯を磨いた。」
「それに」 is conversational. In a report to your boss, a business email or formal writing, it sounds too casual; use 「また」, 「さらに」 or 「加えて」 instead.
「それにしても」 (even so, still) and phrases like 「それに乗る」 or 「それに答える」 (pronoun + particle) are not this conjunction; don't read them as "besides".

daily.title: Recommending a restaurant
daily.description: Listing several good points about a place.
daily.example: That place is cheap, and the portions are big, too.

daily.title: Turning down an invitation
daily.description: A friend invites you, and you give several reasons you can't go.
daily.example: I'm tired today. Besides, I've got homework.

daily.title: Talking about a new home
daily.description: Telling your family what's good about the new place.
daily.example: It's close to the station. And the rooms are spacious, too.

work.title: Explaining your choice
work.description: Telling your boss why you recommend a plan.
work.example: This plan is low-cost. On top of that, we can start right away.

work.title: Talking about a new colleague
work.example: Tanaka-san works fast. And she's very thorough, too.

etymology: Made of the demonstrative 「それ」 + the particle 「に」 expressing addition. Literally "on top of that", it later became fixed as a conjunction.

similar.title: 〜その上 (sentence-initial: moreover)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean "on top of that". 「その上」 is more formal and often adds a step up (even better, or even worse); 「それに」 is conversational and light, and is often used to add another reason.

similar.title: 〜そして (at the start: and then / and also)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both can mean "and also". 「そして」 neutrally lists things or shows sequence, in both speech and writing; 「それに」 only adds one more point in the same direction, never shows sequence, and carries the speaker's evaluation.

similar.title: 〜それから (at the start: after that / also)
similar.explanation: Same root: both are conjunctions made of 「それ」 + a particle. 「それから」 mainly shows time order, or adds one more thing that comes to mind (「それから、牛乳も買ってきて」); 「それに」 piles on evaluations or reasons in the same direction.

similar.title: 〜し
similar.explanation: Similar meaning, and the two are often used together. 「〜し」 lists reasons inside a sentence (「安いし、おいしい」); 「それに」 adds one more at the start of a sentence. They often combine: 「安いし、それにおいしい」.

formation: It is made of the demonstrative 「それ」 + the particle 「に」. 「それ」 points to what was just said, and this 「に」 is the "adding" 「に」 (as in 「AにBを加える」, add B to A). Together they mean "on top of that, add...", so what follows is new information piled onto what came before. Because it's "adding on top", the second part must be of the same kind and point in the same direction; it can't be the opposite, and it can't show time order. Used with reasons, it stacks them one on another, which is why the sentence often ends with 「〜し」 or 「〜から」.

meaning: A sentence-initial conjunction: what came before is the cause, and what follows is the natural result. Also used to urge the other person to keep talking.
connection: Cause sentence. + それで、+ result sentence (often shortened to 「で」 in speech)

senses.label: So / therefore
senses.meaning: The first sentence is a cause or trigger; the second is the result: "so, that's why". Mostly used to explain things that already happened.
senses.connection: Cause A。それで、result B (B usually past tense or an objective fact)
examples: The train stopped. So I was late for the meeting.
I had a fever yesterday. So I stayed home from school.
I love Japanese anime. That's why I started studying Japanese.

senses.label: "And then?"
senses.meaning: While listening, 「それで？」 urges the speaker to go on: "And then? What happened next?" Fairly casual.
senses.connection: それで？／それで、どうなったの？
examples: And then? What happened?
And? Did you end up going?

notes: It can't be followed by a command, request, invitation or intention; use 「だから」 there: ✕「雨だ。それで、傘を持って行きなさい。」→ ○「雨だ。だから、傘を持って行きなさい。」
「それで？」 and its short form 「で？」, used to urge someone on, sound casual; to a boss or client they come across as impatient and rude. Say 「それで、どうなりましたか」 or 「その後はいかがでしたか」 instead.
When apologizing, say 「申し訳ありません」 first and then explain; opening with 「電車が止まって、それで遅れました」 easily sounds like you're making excuses.
「それでは」 (well then), 「それでも」 (even so) and 「それでいい」 (that's fine) all mean different things; don't read them as "so".

daily.title: Explaining why you're late
daily.description: Telling a friend why you're late.
daily.example: The roads were jammed, so I ended up late.

daily.title: Listening to a friend's story
daily.description: Your friend stops halfway and you want to hear the rest.
daily.example: And then? What did he say?

daily.title: Why you started Japanese
daily.description: Giving the reason when introducing yourself.
daily.example: I traveled to Japan, and that got me interested in Japanese.

work.title: Explaining what happened to your boss
work.description: Reporting the cause and result of something.
work.example: The parts didn't arrive. As a result, the work is behind schedule.

work.title: Following up in a meeting
work.description: A boss asks a subordinate to keep explaining.
work.example: So, how did the client react?

etymology: Made of the demonstrative 「それ」 + the particle 「で」 for cause or means. Literally "because of that", it became fixed as a cause-and-effect conjunction.

similar.title: 〜そのため (sentence-initial: therefore / to that end)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express cause and effect. 「そのため」 is more formal and common in news, reports and announcements; 「それで」 is conversational and often used to tell about your own experiences.

similar.title: 〜から (reason)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. Sentence-initial 「だから」 is 「だ」 + 「から」 and carries the speaker's subjective judgment, so it can be followed by a command, request or intention (「だから早く寝なさい」); 「それで」 tends to objectively narrate a cause and effect that already happened, and isn't followed by commands.

similar.title: 〜それから (at the start: after that / also)
similar.explanation: Same root: both are conjunctions made of 「それ」 + a particle. 「それから」 only shows time order (「顔を洗った。それから、朝ご飯を食べた」), with no cause and effect; 「それで」 stresses that the two parts are cause and result.

formation: It is made of the demonstrative 「それ」 + the particle 「で」. 「それ」 points to what was just said, and 「で」 is the 「で」 of cause or occasion (as in 「病気で休む」). Together they mean "because of that", so the second sentence is a natural result of the first. This 「で」 marks a fairly objective cause and lacks the speaker's assertion that 「から」 carries, so 「それで」 is mostly used to narrate causes and effects that already happened, and isn't followed by commands or intentions. In its "urging" use, it means "building on that (what happened next?)", inviting the other person to go on.

meaning: A sentence-initial conjunction showing that what follows goes against what was expected or assumed, with a sense of surprise.
connection: Expectation / premise sentence. + ところが、+ unexpected fact

senses.label: Contrary to expectation
senses.meaning: The first sentence is the speaker's expectation or plan; the second is what actually happened, the opposite: "however, but to my surprise". It carries surprise. The second sentence is usually past tense.
senses.connection: A (expectation / plan)。ところが、B (what actually happened)
examples: The forecast said it would be sunny. But then it started raining in the afternoon.
I thought it would be done quickly. Instead, it took a whole three hours.
I rushed to the station. But the train had already left.

senses.label: Contrary to what's said
senses.meaning: The first sentence is a common view or what others say; the second points out the reality is different: "but actually".
examples: Everyone says it's easy. But when you actually try it, it's hard.
I'd heard it was an expensive place. But it turned out to be surprisingly cheap.

notes: Don't confuse it with 「ところで」 (changing the subject); one sound apart, the meaning is completely different: ✕「簡単だと思った。ところで、難しかった。」→ ○「簡単だと思った。ところが、難しかった。」
The second sentence can only be a fact that has happened or objectively exists; it can't be an intention, command or request: ✕「準備は大変だ。ところが、頑張ろう。」→ ○「準備は大変だ。でも、頑張ろう。」
It can't be used to state your own objection: ✕「その案はいいと思います。ところが、費用が高すぎます。」→ ○「しかし、費用が高すぎます。」

daily.title: A trip that went wrong
daily.description: Telling a friend about a surprise on your trip after you get back.
daily.example: I'd been looking forward to it. But on the day, I came down with a fever.

daily.title: In news and stories
daily.description: Often used in news and stories to introduce a twist.
daily.example: Everyone thought he would pass. But in the end, he failed.

daily.title: Complaining about a purchase
daily.description: Telling your family what you bought wasn't what you expected.
daily.example: I bought it thinking it was big. But it was smaller than I thought.

work.title: Reporting a setback
work.description: Telling your boss something unexpected hit the plan.
work.example: We had been proceeding as planned. However, the other party suddenly contacted us about a change.

work.title: Reporting survey results
work.description: Stating in a report that results were the opposite of the forecast.
work.example: We had expected sales to rise. However, they actually fell.

etymology: Made of the formal noun 「ところ」 ("the moment, the situation") + the conjunctive particle 「が」. It was originally attached to verbs as 「〜たところが」 and later became an independent conjunction, meaning "in that situation, however...".

similar.title: 〜しかし (at the start: however)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express contrast. 「しかし」 is a general "but" and can be used in arguments and to state opinions; 「ところが」 specifically means "the result was the opposite of what was expected", the second sentence must be a fact, and it carries surprise.

similar.title: 〜でも (sentence-initial: but)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「でも」 is the conversational "but" and can also be used to make excuses, push back or state resolve (「でも、頑張る」); 「ところが」 is narrative, stresses surprise, and can't be followed by an intention.

similar.title: 〜ところで (sentence-initial: by the way)
similar.explanation: Same root: both are made of 「ところ」 + a particle. 「ところで」 means "by the way" and changes the subject, with no logical link between the sentences; 「ところが」 means "but, unexpectedly", and the second sentence goes against what the first led you to expect.

similar.title: 〜たところ (result)
similar.explanation: Same root: sentence-initial 「ところが」 originally came from 「〜たところが」 breaking away from the verb before it. 「〜たところ」 follows a verb and means "when I did ..., (I found)", and the result isn't necessarily surprising; sentence-initial 「ところが」 always carries the surprise of an expectation falling through.

formation: It is made of the formal noun 「ところ」 + the conjunctive particle 「が」. 「ところ」 means "the situation, the circumstances" and treats what came before as a situation that has already arisen; 「が」 is the contrastive 「が」. Together they mean "in that situation, however...". It was originally attached to a verb as 「〜たところが」 (did ..., but as it turned out...), then broke away from the verb to become a sentence-initial conjunction. Because it narrates how a situation developed, the second sentence is something that actually happened, which gives it the surprise of an expectation falling through, and it can't take the speaker's intentions or commands. 「ところで」, also built on 「ところ」, uses the 「で」 of setting ("in this situation"), so it became a way to change the subject; the two mean completely different things.
